medical.title: Study shows awake brain mapping can help optimize deep brain stimulation
medical.summary: Awake deep brain stimulation (DBS) surgery can provide information beyond what imaging alone can capture, helping clinicians personalize electrode placement for patients with essential tremor, according to a Mayo Clinic study published in Operative Neurosurgery.

medical.title: Researchers detect signs of neuronal damage in the earliest stage of Huntington's disease
medical.summary: Before motor or cognitive impairments appear and before brain volume loss becomes evident, some individuals carrying the genetic mutation that causes Huntington's disease already show signs of neuronal injury. This is demonstrated by a study conducted by the Institut de Recerca Sant Pau (IR Sant Pau), which has detected elevated levels of neurofilament light chain (NfL), a protein that indicates this damage, in individuals classified in the earliest stage of the disease.

medical.title: Patient comfort with AI-driven health care hinges on provider oversight
medical.summary: More than half of patients (56%) are comfortable with artificial intelligence (AI) making diagnosis or treatment decisions when their health care provider can change or override them, but that figure falls to just 9% when AI makes those decisions without provider review, according to new data from the West Health-Gallup Center on Healthcare in America. The nationally representative survey of more than 5,000 U.S. adults found similar patterns in patient comfort with AI used to interpret diagnostic images or make medication decisions.

medical.title: Experimental drug eliminates 75% of aggressive pancreatic tumors and enhances immune system memory
medical.summary: Many solid tumors, including many cancers of the pancreas, breast, colon and lung, protect themselves with a dense wall of scar-like tissue. That wall keeps the immune system's cancer-killing T cells out. It is a major reason why immunotherapy drugs, which have transformed treatment for some patients, help only a minority of people with solid tumors.

medical.title: Growing older in Japan: Gender and living arrangements linked to mental health
medical.summary: As traditional multigenerational households have become less common, increasing numbers of older adults are living alone or with only their spouses. Over the last few decades, Japan has been experiencing two major demographic changes: a rapidly aging population and a shift in how older adults live. These changes have important implications for health and well-being in later life, as living arrangements can shape social support, companionship and caregiving responsibilities.

medical.title: People worry most about hormone-disrupting chemicals in food and drink, least in skin products, study finds
medical.summary: When it comes to hormone-disrupting chemicals, people worry most about what they eat and drink and least about what they put on their skin, according to new research published in Risk Analysis.

medical.title: Research challenges fusion for lumbar degenerative spondylolisthesis
medical.summary: For adults with lumbar degenerative spondylolisthesis and symptomatic back or leg pain lasting at least three months, the addition of fusion to decompression is not associated with differential effects at 12 months, according to a study published online in the Annals of Internal Medicine.

medical.title: What causes pulmonary fibrosis on a cellular level?
medical.summary: A new UCLA Health study in mice has identified a new potential trigger for pulmonary fibrosis: lipid dysregulation (a fat imbalance) within alveolar macrophages. These are the immune cells that serve as the first line of defense against pathogens and tissue damage. Under normal conditions, they are essential for the maintenance and repair of the lung's airspaces. However, when these cells suffer from a lipid imbalance, they lose their protective qualities, malfunction and begin actively promoting disease.

medical.title: A pillowcase that tracks sleep
medical.summary: An interdisciplinary team of researchers led by Columbia Engineering Associate Professor Xia Zhou has developed PillowSense, a fabric-based sleep-monitoring system. The novel system uses soft sensors to measure heart rate, breathing rate, body movement and sleep posture through natural contact with the sleeper's neck.

medical.title: Researchers identify DNA marker that could predict treatment response in myelodysplastic syndromes
medical.summary: DNA methylation patterns present at diagnosis could help predict which patients with myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) will respond to azacitidine. That's the key finding of a new multicenter study involving researchers at Sylvester Comprehensive Cancer Center, part of the University of Miami Miller School of Medicine.

medical.title: Observations of NICU rounds reveal focus on fluids over nutrients for premature infants
medical.summary: During daily rounds in the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU), physicians need to balance many considerations in their decision-making about nutrition plans for premature infants. Often, instead of discussing how much energy, carbohydrates, fats and protein the baby has received, physicians tend to focus on how much fluid was delivered, according to a study published in Pediatric Research.

medical.title: Mapping Deep South counties links higher diabetes rates to poverty and food insecurity
medical.summary: Counties where residents suffer from higher diabetes rates across the Deep South often also face greater poverty, food insecurity and barriers to health care and physical activity, a new University of Mississippi study reveals.

medical.title: Actor, 85, takes to the stage despite Alzheimer’s diagnosis
medical.summary: Peter Marinker is continuing his stage career after being diagnosed with Alzheimer’s, taking on a role in Samuel Beckett’s Krapp’s Last Tape The post Actor, 85, takes to the stage despite Alzheimer’s diagnosis appeared first on Positive News .

medical.title: Severe premenstrual mood disorder has three subtypes, symptom diaries suggest
medical.summary: Premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD) is a common mood disorder associated with the menstrual cycle. A new study published in Nature Communications shows that PMDD does not follow any universal pattern and that there are three subtypes with different patterns of symptoms. The hope is that this discovery will lead to more individualized treatment.

medical.title: Immune proteins offer new clues to how prostate cancer could be prevented
medical.summary: A new study led by researchers at Oxford Population Health shows that higher levels of proteins involved in activating and coordinating the immune system were associated with a lower risk of developing prostate cancer. The findings suggest that the body's ability to recognize and respond to abnormal cells may play an important role in the early development of prostate cancer and could point to new approaches for preventing the disease.

medical.title: Semaglutide may lower fetal oxygen levels, sheep study suggests
medical.summary: They're the blockbuster drugs transforming weight loss, helping millions of people to shed unwanted kilograms. But while medications such as Ozempic and Wegovy may also improve women's chances of becoming pregnant, what happens to their unborn babies if they continue to take the drugs during pregnancy?

medical.title: Single-tick experiments uncover shifting immune defenses during earliest stages of bacterial infection
medical.summary: Bacteria from the Gulf Coast tick can be transmitted to its host within one hour of attachment before spreading rapidly to lymph nodes and internal tissues, according to new research by a recent graduate of the Frederick P. Whiddon College of Medicine.

medical.title: A brief history of the food pyramid—and its many false starts
medical.summary: The food pyramid has made an unlikely comeback. In January 2026, the U.S. government unveiled an upside-down version, giving prominence to foods such as red meat and full-fat dairy.

medical.title: Scientists discover mysterious “lonely” brain waves linked to memory loss
medical.summary: Scientists have uncovered a surprising link between Alzheimer’s-related protein buildup, disrupted brain waves during deep sleep, and fading memory. The findings suggest that hidden changes in how the brain processes memories overnight may contribute to age-related memory loss long before Alzheimer’s symptoms appear.

medical.title: Goodbye, cavities? Scientists create gel that could regrow tooth enamel
medical.summary: Scientists have developed a revolutionary gel that could regrow lost tooth enamel by harnessing minerals naturally found in saliva, potentially overcoming one of dentistry’s biggest limitations. The regenerated enamel behaves much like healthy enamel, raising hopes for a simple treatment that could repair damaged teeth, prevent decay, and reduce sensitivity.

medical.title: Scientists solve 30-year-old mystery and discover a hidden defense against inflammation
medical.summary: Scientists have solved a decades-old mystery and uncovered a hidden immune system defense that protects healthy cells from the very inflammation meant to fight infections. The surprising discovery could lead to new approaches for treating cancer, inflammatory bowel disease, and other conditions involving excessive inflammation.

medical.title: Scientists finally discover how a common gut bacterium can trigger colon cancer
medical.summary: Scientists at Johns Hopkins have uncovered a crucial missing link between a common gut bacterium and colorectal cancer, solving a mystery that has puzzled researchers for nearly two decades. The bacterium, Bacteroides fragilis, produces a toxin that damages the colon’s protective lining, triggers chronic inflammation, and promotes tumor formation.

medical.title: A surprising vitamin A discovery is changing what scientists know about vision
medical.summary: Scientists at Johns Hopkins University have uncovered a surprising process that helps humans develop sharp vision before birth, challenging decades of assumptions about how the eye forms. Using miniature human retinas grown in the lab, researchers discovered that a vitamin A derivative and thyroid hormones work together to shape the foveola, the tiny region at the center of the retina responsible for our sharpest vision.

medical.title: A simple blood test could reveal Alzheimer’s risk 10 years before symptoms
medical.summary: A major international study found that a simple blood test could help predict Alzheimer’s-related cognitive decline years before symptoms appear, with the highest-risk individuals facing a 38% chance of impairment within five years and an estimated 78% chance within 10 years. Scientists believe the discovery could pave the way for earlier intervention and future treatments designed to prevent Alzheimer’s before memory problems begin.

medical.title: What went right this week: renewed hope for the Brazilian Amazon, plus more
medical.summary: There was renewed hope for the Amazon, a skin cancer vaccine showed promise, and a nicotine loophole was closed in the UK, plus more The post What went right this week: renewed hope for the Brazilian Amazon, plus more appeared first on Positive News .

science.title: Tiny nutrient, big mystery: Key gene reveals how cereal crops transport nickel
science.summary: Nickel plays an important physiological role in plants, but how it is transported over long distances from stems and leaves to grains was poorly understood for more than 50 years. Now researchers have identified a key transporter gene, ZmNAET1, that controls nickel accumulation in cereal grains.

science.title: Changing magnetic dimensionality boosts spin-wave frequency in Cr₂₋δTe₂
science.summary: Magnons are quasiparticles that represent quantized spin waves in magnetic materials. They can carry information without moving electric charge, making them promising for future information technologies that could use less energy than conventional electronics. The frequency, stability and propagation distance of these waves are all important for their potential applications.

science.title: Molecular structures reveal how a bacteriophage protein inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis
science.summary: Drug-resistant bacteria are becoming more common worldwide, posing a major public health challenge. Addressing this problem requires finding new ways to eliminate bacteria, which in turn requires analyzing essential cellular processes that could serve as targets for future antibiotics.

science.title: Neighborhood ties and social connections are linked to high recycling participation
science.summary: Waste separation and recycling are essential to achieving a circular economy and sustainable resource management; however, the long-term success of well-established recycling systems depends on the continued participation of local residents. This study examined how social capital, defined as social relationships characterized by trust, reciprocity and mutual support, is associated with waste separation behavior. The research is published in the Journal of Material Cycles and Waste Management.

science.title: Ice Age camp reveals hunter-gatherers reached Italy thousands of years earlier than previously thought
science.summary: A fresh excavation of the eastern deposit at Riparo Mochi, a rock shelter near today's French–Italian border, has pushed back the timeline for when Ice Age hunter-gatherers from Spain first entered Italy.

science.title: How cells pull together: Theoretical study reveals a hidden source of attraction
science.summary: Imagine two people standing on a stretchy sheet. When one pulls, the other feels the fabric move and responds with a pull of their own. Each adjustment changes what the other feels. Something similar happens between living cells. They tug on the material around them, sense the stretching caused by their neighbors and adjust their own forces.

science.title: Most university students now use AI, but that doesn't mean they like it
science.summary: The university experience has changed drastically since artificial intelligence (AI) became widely available four years ago.

science.title: Team designs molecules that efficiently generate orange-to-red light for OLED displays
science.summary: Most of us spend much of our day staring at organic light-emitting diodes, or OLEDs, which convert electricity into light to produce the colorful displays on smartphones, computer monitors and televisions. Although metal-free light-emitting materials that produce all colors are in demand, it has been difficult to make ones that efficiently emit orange-to-red light. Now, researchers led by the University of Osaka have shown that such materials do not need to be held in a rigid shape to work well: flexible molecules that can change shape can also emit orange-to-red light.

science.title: CHAPEA Crew Leaves a Mark
science.summary: The Crew Health and Performance Exploration Analog (CHAPEA) Mission 2 crew arranged photos around a boot print in the simulated Martian sand outside their habitat on Aug. 31, 2026. The crew recently exited their habitat on Saturday, Oct. 31, after 378 days of isolation in a facility at the agency’s Johnson Space Center in Houston. Health […]

science.title: Study investigates what drivers would pay for 'salmon-safe' tires
science.summary: The average person might be willing to pay a 10% premium for vehicle tires labeled as "salmon safe," according to a new study led by Washington State University.

science.title: A catalyst that protects itself while producing hydrogen
science.summary: Cobalt phosphide (CoP) is a promising alternative to platinum for producing hydrogen from water. However, scientists have struggled to explain why it performs so well. Computer models have suggested that CoP should become unstable under the conditions used to produce hydrogen, yet experiments show that it remains active and durable in acidic, neutral and alkaline environments.

science.title: Simulations cast doubt on unusual asteroid's 'dark comet' status
science.summary: In 2031, Japan's Hayabusa2 spacecraft will arrive at the near-Earth asteroid 1998 KY26: a tiny body that is accelerating in a way that astronomers have struggled to explain. Some studies have suggested that the asteroid is pushed along by water escaping from it as gas, making it an as-yet theoretical "dark comet."

science.title: A new role for chlorine: Uncovering anion redox in solid-state battery cathodes
science.summary: As demand grows for safer and more capable rechargeable batteries, scientists are looking beyond the familiar metal-centered chemistry of conventional cathodes. A promising route is to draw additional charge from anions—the negatively charged atoms in a material—rather than relying on transition metals alone. Oxygen and sulfur have attracted substantial attention in this area. Whether chlorine can play a comparable role in chloride-based battery cathodes has been less clear.

science.title: Scientists release large-scale in situ cryo-ET resource for mouse sperm ultrastructure
science.summary: The scale, quality and regional coverage of public cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) data resources have been insufficient, severely limiting data reuse, cross-regional comparisons and the development of automated analysis methods. A new resource aims to help fill that gap, providing 1,413 reconstructed tomograms and associated data from wild-type C57BL/6J mouse sperm.

science.title: World's most sensitive lab-based axion search presents its first results
science.summary: Physicists at the ALPS II collaboration have reported the first results from the Any-Light-Particle-Search (ALPS) II experiment: the most sensitive instrument of its kind in the search for hypothetical "axions." Headed by Axel Lindner at the DESY Research Centre in Germany, the collaboration found no evidence for axions in this initial campaign, but its results offer valuable guidance for future runs: tightening the search for one of the most promising candidates for dark matter.

science.title: Egyptian cats meant for the gods led harsh lives, extensive museum collection reveals
science.summary: More than 2,000 years ago, Egyptians offered cats to the gods. Now, a new study published in the Journal of Archaeological Science suggests that even cats destined for the gods did not necessarily live pampered lives.

science.title: Student team develops innovative 'Trojan horse' in the fight against the Asian hornet
science.summary: An interdisciplinary team of students from the Vrije Universiteit Brussel (VUB) is taking part in iGEM, the international synthetic biology competition in Paris (Nov. 13–16), this fall. Using a clever combination of artificial intelligence, a mechanical trap and protein nanofibers, they are presenting a targeted method to efficiently control populations of the Asian hornet.

science.title: What seal pups can reveal about the effects of mercury exposure
science.summary: Marine mammals living along the Pacific Coast of North America encounter more than the fish, crustaceans, cephalopods and other marine mammals that live around them. Because contaminants such as mercury can move through marine food webs and biomagnify—becoming more concentrated as they move from prey to predator—fish-eating marine mammals can be exposed to higher levels of these pollutants.

science.title: Researchers launch all-out assault on sawflies damaging wheat crops
science.summary: Colorado wheat—the foundation for flour used in bread, noodles and pastries—has been besieged by the wheat stem sawfly, a native insect that recently developed a preference for wheat over native grasses. This destructive agricultural pest has spread across the state's Eastern Plains, devastating fields where it takes hold and causing $70 million in direct and indirect losses a year to one of Colorado's top agricultural commodities.

science.title: Turkish province despairs at being Europe's plastic dump
science.summary: At first glance, the canal near which Ibrahim Yildiz grazes his sheep in the southern Adana province appears idyllic, framed by rows of clementine trees—until the mountains of plastic shavings come into view.

science.title: Quantum could solve AI energy drain, says tech founder
science.summary: Quantum computers could curb the vast energy demands of artificial intelligence data centers with their ability to run complex calculations, one of the tech's pioneers told AFP.

science.title: Making metal–organic frameworks easier to shape for electronic devices
science.summary: In 1974, the University of Melbourne's chemistry professor Richard Robson had the idea of replacing the wooden balls and metal rods used in structural models with molecules and chemical bonds. He began experimenting with copper ions linked by a four-armed organic molecule, creating a structure with a cavity. His work laid the foundation for metal–organic frameworks (MOFs), a class of porous materials formed by linking metal ions with organic molecules. Their pores can capture pollutants, support chemical reactions and store gases, giving MOFs a wide range of potential applications.

science.title: Digging up the past can change the ground beneath it
science.summary: Archaeological excavation uncovers the past but also changes the landscape that has preserved sites for centuries or millennia. These changes influence water flow, soil erosion and the stability of exposed remains. Researchers from Istanbul Technical University and the U.S. have shown how computer models can assist archaeologists in understanding and planning for these effects, especially regarding erosion risks. Using an Early Bronze Age settlement in Türkiye as a case study, they reconstructed the landscape before and after excavation.

environment.title: Amazon mapping shows cacao expansion without deforestation in Brazil
environment.summary: While West Africa clears rainforest for chocolate, Brazilian farmers are reviving degraded pastures.

environment.title: Money laundering complaints target JBS, Barclays over profits linked to illegal deforestation
environment.summary: A coalition of legal and environmental groups has filed money laundering complaints against JBS, the world’s largest meat processor, and 12 financial institutions, investors and advisers, including the U.K. bank Barclays. The complaints allegedly tie JBS profits to illegal deforestation in the Brazilian Amazon. The Transnational Legal Coalition filed 14 complaints with prosecutors and financial […]

environment.title: 3M agrees to pay more than $7 billion to settle ‘forever chemical’ groundwater contamination claims
environment.summary: Chemical manufacturer 3M will pay up to $7.35 billion to settle lawsuits by people who say they were sickened by groundwater contamination from compounds used in firefighting foam and other consumer products. The St. Paul, Minnesota-based company announced the settlement Tuesday. It will pay the money over nine years to as many as 120,000 people […]

environment.title: How Ghana’s new license to sell sustainable timber improves institutions & cooperation (analysis)
environment.summary: When Ghana began its Voluntary Partnership Agreement (VPA) process with the European Union, the attraction was clear. Europe is an important market for Ghanaian timber, international expectations around its legality were changing, and the VPA offered both market access and support for strengthening national forest governance. After a 16-year journey, last year Ghana became the […]

environment.title: A train was delayed by a solar storm. But something didn't add up.
environment.summary: Scientists have cracked a 178-year-old mystery surrounding a train delayed by a solar storm, revealing that the famous incident happened in 1848 rather than 1841. The discovery rewrites the early history of space weather and highlights a threat that still endangers modern power grids, satellites, and communication systems.

environment.title: A massive asteroid slammed into the North Sea and unleashed a 330-foot tsunami
environment.summary: A decades-long mystery beneath the North Sea has finally been solved. Scientists have confirmed that the Silverpit Crater, buried 700 meters below the seabed, was created when a 160-meter-wide asteroid struck Earth roughly 43 to 46 million years ago. The violent collision blasted a towering curtain of rock and water 1.5 kilometers into the air and triggered a tsunami more than 100 meters high.

environment.title: Scientists discover ghostly, eyeless creature hidden in Chinese cave
environment.summary: Deep inside a high-altitude Chinese cave, scientists discovered a ghostly, eyeless freshwater snail that has evolved to live entirely in darkness, marking the first recorded discovery of its kind in China. Named after a faceless mythical creature, the rare species may already be in danger, with researchers finding only three living adults.

environment.title: Scientists discover a plastic-eating “Pac-Man” enzyme with a surprising secret
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered a remarkable “Pac-Man enzyme” that helps bacteria devour certain types of plastic and may offer new hope in the fight against plastic pollution. Researchers found that several biodegradable plastics completely broke down in soil within about a year, while conventional plastic remained largely unchanged.

environment.title: “Crawzilla” was huge. Then scientists found an even bigger crayfish
environment.summary: A nationwide search for giant crayfish uncovered a record-breaking Tennessee specimen and a surprising mystery about how big these freshwater creatures can grow. Scientists found that North American crayfish seem to hit a biological size limit, possibly because of their muscles or protective shells.

mix_items.summary: Un liceu din centrul Craiovei a fost evacuat după ce o conductă de gaze a fost spartă de muncitori. La fața locului intervin angajați ai distribuitorului de gaze, pompieri și polițiști.

mix_items.summary: Cercetătorii de la Universitatea RMIT din Australia au dezvoltat o metodă prin care zațul de cafea poate fi transformat într-un material utilizat la producerea betonului, cu o rezistență cu până la...

mix_items.summary: Descoperă povestea lui Darius și cum sprijinul educațional oferit de Fundația Inocenți l-a ajutat să capete încredere în sine și să își urmeze visurile. The post De la timiditate la încredere: povestea unui tânăr care îndrăznește să viseze appeared first on Fundația Inocenți .

mix_items.title: Tiny nutrient, big mystery: Key gene reveals how cereal crops transport nickel
mix_items.summary: Nickel plays an important physiological role in plants, but how it is transported over long distances from stems and leaves to grains was poorly understood for more than 50 years. Now researchers have identified a key transporter gene, ZmNAET1, that controls nickel accumulation in cereal grains.

mix_items.title: Changing magnetic dimensionality boosts spin-wave frequency in Cr₂₋δTe₂
mix_items.summary: Magnons are quasiparticles that represent quantized spin waves in magnetic materials. They can carry information without moving electric charge, making them promising for future information technologies that could use less energy than conventional electronics. The frequency, stability and propagation distance of these waves are all important for their potential applications.

mix_items.title: Sute de copii sprijiniți prin educație nonformală de Inocenți și Pepco
mix_items.summary: Peste 500 de copii au participat la activități de educație nonformală și wellbeing derulate de Fundația Inocenți cu sprijinul Pepco România. The post Sute de copii sprijiniți prin educație nonformală de Inocenți și Pepco appeared first on Fundația Inocenți .

mix_items.title: Molecular structures reveal how a bacteriophage protein inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis
mix_items.summary: Drug-resistant bacteria are becoming more common worldwide, posing a major public health challenge. Addressing this problem requires finding new ways to eliminate bacteria, which in turn requires analyzing essential cellular processes that could serve as targets for future antibiotics.

mix_items.title: Neighborhood ties and social connections are linked to high recycling participation
mix_items.summary: Waste separation and recycling are essential to achieving a circular economy and sustainable resource management; however, the long-term success of well-established recycling systems depends on the continued participation of local residents. This study examined how social capital, defined as social relationships characterized by trust, reciprocity and mutual support, is associated with waste separation behavior. The research is published in the Journal of Material Cycles and Waste Management.

mix_items.title: Ice Age camp reveals hunter-gatherers reached Italy thousands of years earlier than previously thought
mix_items.summary: A fresh excavation of the eastern deposit at Riparo Mochi, a rock shelter near today's French–Italian border, has pushed back the timeline for when Ice Age hunter-gatherers from Spain first entered Italy.

mix_items.title: Study shows awake brain mapping can help optimize deep brain stimulation
mix_items.summary: Awake deep brain stimulation (DBS) surgery can provide information beyond what imaging alone can capture, helping clinicians personalize electrode placement for patients with essential tremor, according to a Mayo Clinic study published in Operative Neurosurgery.

mix_items.title: How cells pull together: Theoretical study reveals a hidden source of attraction
mix_items.summary: Imagine two people standing on a stretchy sheet. When one pulls, the other feels the fabric move and responds with a pull of their own. Each adjustment changes what the other feels. Something similar happens between living cells. They tug on the material around them, sense the stretching caused by their neighbors and adjust their own forces.

mix_items.title: Most university students now use AI, but that doesn't mean they like it
mix_items.summary: The university experience has changed drastically since artificial intelligence (AI) became widely available four years ago.

mix_items.title: Team designs molecules that efficiently generate orange-to-red light for OLED displays
mix_items.summary: Most of us spend much of our day staring at organic light-emitting diodes, or OLEDs, which convert electricity into light to produce the colorful displays on smartphones, computer monitors and televisions. Although metal-free light-emitting materials that produce all colors are in demand, it has been difficult to make ones that efficiently emit orange-to-red light. Now, researchers led by the University of Osaka have shown that such materials do not need to be held in a rigid shape to work well: flexible molecules that can change shape can also emit orange-to-red light.

mix_items.title: Researchers detect signs of neuronal damage in the earliest stage of Huntington's disease
mix_items.summary: Before motor or cognitive impairments appear and before brain volume loss becomes evident, some individuals carrying the genetic mutation that causes Huntington's disease already show signs of neuronal injury. This is demonstrated by a study conducted by the Institut de Recerca Sant Pau (IR Sant Pau), which has detected elevated levels of neurofilament light chain (NfL), a protein that indicates this damage, in individuals classified in the earliest stage of the disease.

mix_items.summary: The Crew Health and Performance Exploration Analog (CHAPEA) Mission 2 crew arranged photos around a boot print in the simulated Martian sand outside their habitat on Aug. 31, 2026. The crew recently exited their habitat on Saturday, Oct. 31, after 378 days of isolation in a facility at the agency’s Johnson Space Center in Houston. Health […]

mix_items.title: Patient comfort with AI-driven health care hinges on provider oversight
mix_items.summary: More than half of patients (56%) are comfortable with artificial intelligence (AI) making diagnosis or treatment decisions when their health care provider can change or override them, but that figure falls to just 9% when AI makes those decisions without provider review, according to new data from the West Health-Gallup Center on Healthcare in America. The nationally representative survey of more than 5,000 U.S. adults found similar patterns in patient comfort with AI used to interpret diagnostic images or make medication decisions.

mix_items.title: Study investigates what drivers would pay for 'salmon-safe' tires
mix_items.summary: The average person might be willing to pay a 10% premium for vehicle tires labeled as "salmon safe," according to a new study led by Washington State University.

mix_items.title: A catalyst that protects itself while producing hydrogen
mix_items.summary: Cobalt phosphide (CoP) is a promising alternative to platinum for producing hydrogen from water. However, scientists have struggled to explain why it performs so well. Computer models have suggested that CoP should become unstable under the conditions used to produce hydrogen, yet experiments show that it remains active and durable in acidic, neutral and alkaline environments.

mix_items.title: Experimental drug eliminates 75% of aggressive pancreatic tumors and enhances immune system memory
mix_items.summary: Many solid tumors, including many cancers of the pancreas, breast, colon and lung, protect themselves with a dense wall of scar-like tissue. That wall keeps the immune system's cancer-killing T cells out. It is a major reason why immunotherapy drugs, which have transformed treatment for some patients, help only a minority of people with solid tumors.

mix_items.title: Simulations cast doubt on unusual asteroid's 'dark comet' status
mix_items.summary: In 2031, Japan's Hayabusa2 spacecraft will arrive at the near-Earth asteroid 1998 KY26: a tiny body that is accelerating in a way that astronomers have struggled to explain. Some studies have suggested that the asteroid is pushed along by water escaping from it as gas, making it an as-yet theoretical "dark comet."

mix_items.title: Growing older in Japan: Gender and living arrangements linked to mental health
mix_items.summary: As traditional multigenerational households have become less common, increasing numbers of older adults are living alone or with only their spouses. Over the last few decades, Japan has been experiencing two major demographic changes: a rapidly aging population and a shift in how older adults live. These changes have important implications for health and well-being in later life, as living arrangements can shape social support, companionship and caregiving responsibilities.

mix_items.title: A new role for chlorine: Uncovering anion redox in solid-state battery cathodes
mix_items.summary: As demand grows for safer and more capable rechargeable batteries, scientists are looking beyond the familiar metal-centered chemistry of conventional cathodes. A promising route is to draw additional charge from anions—the negatively charged atoms in a material—rather than relying on transition metals alone. Oxygen and sulfur have attracted substantial attention in this area. Whether chlorine can play a comparable role in chloride-based battery cathodes has been less clear.

mix_items.title: Scientists release large-scale in situ cryo-ET resource for mouse sperm ultrastructure
mix_items.summary: The scale, quality and regional coverage of public cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) data resources have been insufficient, severely limiting data reuse, cross-regional comparisons and the development of automated analysis methods. A new resource aims to help fill that gap, providing 1,413 reconstructed tomograms and associated data from wild-type C57BL/6J mouse sperm.

mix_items.title: People worry most about hormone-disrupting chemicals in food and drink, least in skin products, study finds
mix_items.summary: When it comes to hormone-disrupting chemicals, people worry most about what they eat and drink and least about what they put on their skin, according to new research published in Risk Analysis.

mix_items.title: World's most sensitive lab-based axion search presents its first results
mix_items.summary: Physicists at the ALPS II collaboration have reported the first results from the Any-Light-Particle-Search (ALPS) II experiment: the most sensitive instrument of its kind in the search for hypothetical "axions." Headed by Axel Lindner at the DESY Research Centre in Germany, the collaboration found no evidence for axions in this initial campaign, but its results offer valuable guidance for future runs: tightening the search for one of the most promising candidates for dark matter.

mix_items.title: Research challenges fusion for lumbar degenerative spondylolisthesis
mix_items.summary: For adults with lumbar degenerative spondylolisthesis and symptomatic back or leg pain lasting at least three months, the addition of fusion to decompression is not associated with differential effects at 12 months, according to a study published online in the Annals of Internal Medicine.

mix_items.title: Egyptian cats meant for the gods led harsh lives, extensive museum collection reveals
mix_items.summary: More than 2,000 years ago, Egyptians offered cats to the gods. Now, a new study published in the Journal of Archaeological Science suggests that even cats destined for the gods did not necessarily live pampered lives.

mix_items.title: Student team develops innovative 'Trojan horse' in the fight against the Asian hornet
mix_items.summary: An interdisciplinary team of students from the Vrije Universiteit Brussel (VUB) is taking part in iGEM, the international synthetic biology competition in Paris (Nov. 13–16), this fall. Using a clever combination of artificial intelligence, a mechanical trap and protein nanofibers, they are presenting a targeted method to efficiently control populations of the Asian hornet.

mix_items.title: What causes pulmonary fibrosis on a cellular level?
mix_items.summary: A new UCLA Health study in mice has identified a new potential trigger for pulmonary fibrosis: lipid dysregulation (a fat imbalance) within alveolar macrophages. These are the immune cells that serve as the first line of defense against pathogens and tissue damage. Under normal conditions, they are essential for the maintenance and repair of the lung's airspaces. However, when these cells suffer from a lipid imbalance, they lose their protective qualities, malfunction and begin actively promoting disease.

mix_items.title: A pillowcase that tracks sleep
mix_items.summary: An interdisciplinary team of researchers led by Columbia Engineering Associate Professor Xia Zhou has developed PillowSense, a fabric-based sleep-monitoring system. The novel system uses soft sensors to measure heart rate, breathing rate, body movement and sleep posture through natural contact with the sleeper's neck.

mix_items.title: What seal pups can reveal about the effects of mercury exposure
mix_items.summary: Marine mammals living along the Pacific Coast of North America encounter more than the fish, crustaceans, cephalopods and other marine mammals that live around them. Because contaminants such as mercury can move through marine food webs and biomagnify—becoming more concentrated as they move from prey to predator—fish-eating marine mammals can be exposed to higher levels of these pollutants.

mix_items.title: Researchers identify DNA marker that could predict treatment response in myelodysplastic syndromes
mix_items.summary: DNA methylation patterns present at diagnosis could help predict which patients with myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) will respond to azacitidine. That's the key finding of a new multicenter study involving researchers at Sylvester Comprehensive Cancer Center, part of the University of Miami Miller School of Medicine.

mix_items.title: Observations of NICU rounds reveal focus on fluids over nutrients for premature infants
mix_items.summary: During daily rounds in the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU), physicians need to balance many considerations in their decision-making about nutrition plans for premature infants. Often, instead of discussing how much energy, carbohydrates, fats and protein the baby has received, physicians tend to focus on how much fluid was delivered, according to a study published in Pediatric Research.

mix_items.title: Mapping Deep South counties links higher diabetes rates to poverty and food insecurity
mix_items.summary: Counties where residents suffer from higher diabetes rates across the Deep South often also face greater poverty, food insecurity and barriers to health care and physical activity, a new University of Mississippi study reveals.

mix_items.title: Researchers launch all-out assault on sawflies damaging wheat crops
mix_items.summary: Colorado wheat—the foundation for flour used in bread, noodles and pastries—has been besieged by the wheat stem sawfly, a native insect that recently developed a preference for wheat over native grasses. This destructive agricultural pest has spread across the state's Eastern Plains, devastating fields where it takes hold and causing $70 million in direct and indirect losses a year to one of Colorado's top agricultural commodities.

mix_items.title: Turkish province despairs at being Europe's plastic dump
mix_items.summary: At first glance, the canal near which Ibrahim Yildiz grazes his sheep in the southern Adana province appears idyllic, framed by rows of clementine trees—until the mountains of plastic shavings come into view.

mix_items.title: Actor, 85, takes to the stage despite Alzheimer’s diagnosis
mix_items.summary: Peter Marinker is continuing his stage career after being diagnosed with Alzheimer’s, taking on a role in Samuel Beckett’s Krapp’s Last Tape The post Actor, 85, takes to the stage despite Alzheimer’s diagnosis appeared first on Positive News .

mix_items.title: Quantum could solve AI energy drain, says tech founder
mix_items.summary: Quantum computers could curb the vast energy demands of artificial intelligence data centers with their ability to run complex calculations, one of the tech's pioneers told AFP.

mix_items.title: Severe premenstrual mood disorder has three subtypes, symptom diaries suggest
mix_items.summary: Premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD) is a common mood disorder associated with the menstrual cycle. A new study published in Nature Communications shows that PMDD does not follow any universal pattern and that there are three subtypes with different patterns of symptoms. The hope is that this discovery will lead to more individualized treatment.

mix_items.title: Making metal–organic frameworks easier to shape for electronic devices
mix_items.summary: In 1974, the University of Melbourne's chemistry professor Richard Robson had the idea of replacing the wooden balls and metal rods used in structural models with molecules and chemical bonds. He began experimenting with copper ions linked by a four-armed organic molecule, creating a structure with a cavity. His work laid the foundation for metal–organic frameworks (MOFs), a class of porous materials formed by linking metal ions with organic molecules. Their pores can capture pollutants, support chemical reactions and store gases, giving MOFs a wide range of potential applications.

mix_items.title: Immune proteins offer new clues to how prostate cancer could be prevented
mix_items.summary: A new study led by researchers at Oxford Population Health shows that higher levels of proteins involved in activating and coordinating the immune system were associated with a lower risk of developing prostate cancer. The findings suggest that the body's ability to recognize and respond to abnormal cells may play an important role in the early development of prostate cancer and could point to new approaches for preventing the disease.

mix_items.title: Digging up the past can change the ground beneath it
mix_items.summary: Archaeological excavation uncovers the past but also changes the landscape that has preserved sites for centuries or millennia. These changes influence water flow, soil erosion and the stability of exposed remains. Researchers from Istanbul Technical University and the U.S. have shown how computer models can assist archaeologists in understanding and planning for these effects, especially regarding erosion risks. Using an Early Bronze Age settlement in Türkiye as a case study, they reconstructed the landscape before and after excavation.

mix_items.title: Semaglutide may lower fetal oxygen levels, sheep study suggests
mix_items.summary: They're the blockbuster drugs transforming weight loss, helping millions of people to shed unwanted kilograms. But while medications such as Ozempic and Wegovy may also improve women's chances of becoming pregnant, what happens to their unborn babies if they continue to take the drugs during pregnancy?

mix_items.title: Single-tick experiments uncover shifting immune defenses during earliest stages of bacterial infection
mix_items.summary: Bacteria from the Gulf Coast tick can be transmitted to its host within one hour of attachment before spreading rapidly to lymph nodes and internal tissues, according to new research by a recent graduate of the Frederick P. Whiddon College of Medicine.

mix_items.title: A brief history of the food pyramid—and its many false starts
mix_items.summary: The food pyramid has made an unlikely comeback. In January 2026, the U.S. government unveiled an upside-down version, giving prominence to foods such as red meat and full-fat dairy.

mix_items.title: Amazon mapping shows cacao expansion without deforestation in Brazil
mix_items.summary: While West Africa clears rainforest for chocolate, Brazilian farmers are reviving degraded pastures.

mix_items.title: Money laundering complaints target JBS, Barclays over profits linked to illegal deforestation
mix_items.summary: A coalition of legal and environmental groups has filed money laundering complaints against JBS, the world’s largest meat processor, and 12 financial institutions, investors and advisers, including the U.K. bank Barclays. The complaints allegedly tie JBS profits to illegal deforestation in the Brazilian Amazon. The Transnational Legal Coalition filed 14 complaints with prosecutors and financial […]

mix_items.title: 3M agrees to pay more than $7 billion to settle ‘forever chemical’ groundwater contamination claims
mix_items.summary: Chemical manufacturer 3M will pay up to $7.35 billion to settle lawsuits by people who say they were sickened by groundwater contamination from compounds used in firefighting foam and other consumer products. The St. Paul, Minnesota-based company announced the settlement Tuesday. It will pay the money over nine years to as many as 120,000 people […]

mix_items.title: How Ghana’s new license to sell sustainable timber improves institutions & cooperation (analysis)
mix_items.summary: When Ghana began its Voluntary Partnership Agreement (VPA) process with the European Union, the attraction was clear. Europe is an important market for Ghanaian timber, international expectations around its legality were changing, and the VPA offered both market access and support for strengthening national forest governance. After a 16-year journey, last year Ghana became the […]

mix_items.title: Scientists discover mysterious “lonely” brain waves linked to memory loss
mix_items.summary: Scientists have uncovered a surprising link between Alzheimer’s-related protein buildup, disrupted brain waves during deep sleep, and fading memory. The findings suggest that hidden changes in how the brain processes memories overnight may contribute to age-related memory loss long before Alzheimer’s symptoms appear.

mix_items.title: Goodbye, cavities? Scientists create gel that could regrow tooth enamel
mix_items.summary: Scientists have developed a revolutionary gel that could regrow lost tooth enamel by harnessing minerals naturally found in saliva, potentially overcoming one of dentistry’s biggest limitations. The regenerated enamel behaves much like healthy enamel, raising hopes for a simple treatment that could repair damaged teeth, prevent decay, and reduce sensitivity.

mix_items.title: Scientists solve 30-year-old mystery and discover a hidden defense against inflammation
mix_items.summary: Scientists have solved a decades-old mystery and uncovered a hidden immune system defense that protects healthy cells from the very inflammation meant to fight infections. The surprising discovery could lead to new approaches for treating cancer, inflammatory bowel disease, and other conditions involving excessive inflammation.

mix_items.title: Scientists finally discover how a common gut bacterium can trigger colon cancer
mix_items.summary: Scientists at Johns Hopkins have uncovered a crucial missing link between a common gut bacterium and colorectal cancer, solving a mystery that has puzzled researchers for nearly two decades. The bacterium, Bacteroides fragilis, produces a toxin that damages the colon’s protective lining, triggers chronic inflammation, and promotes tumor formation.

mix_items.title: A surprising vitamin A discovery is changing what scientists know about vision
mix_items.summary: Scientists at Johns Hopkins University have uncovered a surprising process that helps humans develop sharp vision before birth, challenging decades of assumptions about how the eye forms. Using miniature human retinas grown in the lab, researchers discovered that a vitamin A derivative and thyroid hormones work together to shape the foveola, the tiny region at the center of the retina responsible for our sharpest vision.

mix_items.title: A simple blood test could reveal Alzheimer’s risk 10 years before symptoms
mix_items.summary: A major international study found that a simple blood test could help predict Alzheimer’s-related cognitive decline years before symptoms appear, with the highest-risk individuals facing a 38% chance of impairment within five years and an estimated 78% chance within 10 years. Scientists believe the discovery could pave the way for earlier intervention and future treatments designed to prevent Alzheimer’s before memory problems begin.

mix_items.title: What went right this week: renewed hope for the Brazilian Amazon, plus more
mix_items.summary: There was renewed hope for the Amazon, a skin cancer vaccine showed promise, and a nicotine loophole was closed in the UK, plus more The post What went right this week: renewed hope for the Brazilian Amazon, plus more appeared first on Positive News .

mix_items.title: A train was delayed by a solar storm. But something didn't add up.
mix_items.summary: Scientists have cracked a 178-year-old mystery surrounding a train delayed by a solar storm, revealing that the famous incident happened in 1848 rather than 1841. The discovery rewrites the early history of space weather and highlights a threat that still endangers modern power grids, satellites, and communication systems.

mix_items.title: A massive asteroid slammed into the North Sea and unleashed a 330-foot tsunami
mix_items.summary: A decades-long mystery beneath the North Sea has finally been solved. Scientists have confirmed that the Silverpit Crater, buried 700 meters below the seabed, was created when a 160-meter-wide asteroid struck Earth roughly 43 to 46 million years ago. The violent collision blasted a towering curtain of rock and water 1.5 kilometers into the air and triggered a tsunami more than 100 meters high.

mix_items.title: Scientists discover ghostly, eyeless creature hidden in Chinese cave
mix_items.summary: Deep inside a high-altitude Chinese cave, scientists discovered a ghostly, eyeless freshwater snail that has evolved to live entirely in darkness, marking the first recorded discovery of its kind in China. Named after a faceless mythical creature, the rare species may already be in danger, with researchers finding only three living adults.

mix_items.title: Scientists discover a plastic-eating “Pac-Man” enzyme with a surprising secret
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered a remarkable “Pac-Man enzyme” that helps bacteria devour certain types of plastic and may offer new hope in the fight against plastic pollution. Researchers found that several biodegradable plastics completely broke down in soil within about a year, while conventional plastic remained largely unchanged.

mix_items.title: “Crawzilla” was huge. Then scientists found an even bigger crayfish
mix_items.summary: A nationwide search for giant crayfish uncovered a record-breaking Tennessee specimen and a surprising mystery about how big these freshwater creatures can grow. Scientists found that North American crayfish seem to hit a biological size limit, possibly because of their muscles or protective shells.
